content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has released updated guidelines for the screening and treatment of cervical pre-cancer lesions to prevent cervical cancer. This second edition emphasizes the use of messenger RNA (mRNA) tests for detecting high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) types. These guidelines aim to improve cervical cancer prevention strategies globally, particularly in regions with high disease burden, such as sub-Saharan Africa, Melanesia, South America, and Southeast Asia. Cervical cancer remains a leading cause of mortality among women, with an estimated 604,000 new cases and 342,000 deaths worldwide in 2020. It is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in 23 countries and the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in 36 countries. In response, WHO launched a Global Strategy in 2020 to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem. The strategy includes ambitious targets for 2030: achieving 90% HPV vaccination coverage among eligible girls, 70% screening coverage with high-performance tests, and ensuring 90% of women with positive screening results or cervical lesions receive appropriate treatment. The updated guidelines focus on two approaches to cervical cancer screening and treatment. The screen-and-treat approach bases treatment decisions solely on a positive primary screening test, while the screen, triage, and treat approach involves a secondary test (triage) to confirm the need for treatment. HPV mRNA testing, which detects the E6/E7 oncogenic proteins responsible for HPV-mediated transformation of epithelial cells, is presented as an alternative to HPV DNA testing. mRNA tests may offer greater specificity by correlating with active viral replication, which is further along the pathway to pre-cancerous changes. The guidelines recommend HPV mRNA testing as a primary screening method for the general population of women, with or without triage, using samples collected by healthcare providers. Screening intervals of five years are suggested. However, HPV DNA testing remains the preferred method, and mRNA testing is considered a conditional recommendation based on low-certainty evidence. No specific recommendations were made for women living with HIV due to insufficient evidence on the outcomes of mRNA testing in this population. The development of these guidelines followed WHO's rigorous methodology, including systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and modeling to evaluate the accuracy, impact, and cost-effectiveness of different screening and treatment strategies. The Aptima™ mRNA assay, which detects E6/E7 mRNA from 14 high-risk HPV types, is currently the most widely documented mRNA testing technology. It provides pooled detection of high-risk HPV types but does not differentiate individual genotypes. A separate assay is available for detecting specific genotypes like HPV 16, 18, and 45. The guidelines also highlight the importance of integrating cervical cancer prevention into broader health and gender equality goals, as outlined in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). By updating national protocols and simplifying screening algorithms, countries can enhance access to effective screening and treatment, ultimately reducing the global burden of cervical cancer.
